title: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, CHILDBIRTH, AND BLEEDING—WHY ARE CHRISTIANS EMBARRASSED TO?
paragraphs: THE BIBLE TALKS ABOUT SEX, SEMEN, MENSTRUATION, CHILDBIRTH, AND BLEEDING—WHY ARE CHRISTIANS EMBARRASSED TO?

We have sometimes made people ashamed of subjects God was never ashamed to address—and somewhere between our silence and their questions, an entire generation learned to search everywhere except Scripture.
There are words some Christians can say comfortably from a pulpit.
Parents wonder whether the children should be listening.

Church people who can discuss murder, adultery, crucifixion, demons, betrayal, war, drunkenness, and hell without blinking suddenly become uncomfortable when the conversation turns toward the human body.
And yet there is an uncomfortable question hiding inside that discomfort:
If God was not embarrassed to put these subjects in His Word...
why are we embarrassed to talk about them?
Open Leviticus 15 and the Hebrew does not whisper.
Speaking of a man's seminal emission, the text says:
Literally, language referring to an emission of seed—semen.
The Hebrew verse itself reads in part:
“And if a man has an emission of semen...” (Leviticus 15:16).
That isn't modern culture inserting sexuality into Scripture.
The same chapter speaks directly about a woman's menstrual bleeding. Leviticus 15:19 discusses a woman whose bodily discharge is blood and places it within Israel's laws concerning ritual purity.
Leviticus 12 speaks about pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum purification, and blood.
Its Hebrew begins the instruction concerning childbirth with:
A woman conceives and gives birth.
The Bible is astonishingly unafraid of the body.
And bodies becoming old and dying.
God created human beings as embodied creatures. The biblical story does not present spirituality as an escape from having a body. The scandal of Christianity goes even further:
“The Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.” (John 1:14, KJV)
The eternal Son entered our physical world.
Jesus did not save humanity from a safe theological distance.
And He rose bodily from the grave.
Christianity is not embarrassed by embodiment at its center.
It is built around the astonishing declaration that the Son of God took on flesh.
So perhaps the problem was never that these subjects were too physical for Christianity.
Perhaps sometimes our Christianity became too embarrassed to sound like the Bible.
Because when churches refuse to speak truthfully about sex, children do not stop becoming curious.
Teenagers do not stop experiencing desire.
Married couples do not stop struggling with intimacy.
People do not stop experiencing infertility.
Mothers do not stop bleeding after childbirth.
Men do not stop wrestling with sexual temptation.
Victims do not stop carrying wounds from sexual abuse.
We simply surrender the conversation to somebody else.
And somebody else is always willing to disciple the silence.
Pornography will teach what the church refuses to discuss.
And then Christians sometimes wonder why people know the world's vocabulary for sexuality better than they know God's design for the body.
But there is another mistake we must avoid.
We cannot read words like “unclean” in Leviticus and casually conclude that menstruation, childbirth, or every seminal emission was therefore a personal moral sin.
That collapses categories the text itself distinguishes.

Leviticus 11–15 deals substantially with ritual purity, while later chapters address moral prohibitions. Biblical scholarship regularly notes this distinction: ritual impurity could arise through ordinary realities of embodied life and was not automatically an accusation of personal wickedness.
A woman was not sinful because she menstruated.
A mother had not committed moral evil because she gave birth.
A man was not automatically guilty of moral rebellion simply because his body emitted semen.
“Unclean” in these passages cannot simply be substituted with “sinful.”
Because countless people have carried shame God never commanded them to carry.
Some woman reading this learned as a girl to hate the changing body God gave her.
Some man reading this was never taught the difference between involuntary bodily function and chosen lust, so shame swallowed everything.
Someone grew up believing every conversation about sex was dirty.
Someone was abused and somehow came away feeling as though their body was the shameful thing.
Someone committed genuine sexual sin and has spent years hiding because Christians taught condemnation far more convincingly than they taught restoration.
Someone is married and still feels guilty about enjoying the intimacy God designed for covenant marriage.
Someone is single and ashamed that sexual desire exists at all, instead of learning how desire can be governed faithfully rather than worshiped or feared.
And someone is reading this with a history they desperately hope nobody discovers.
That is where this conversation stops being merely about anatomy.
Because eventually every conversation about human shame walks toward Jesus.
There was once a woman who had been bleeding for twelve years.
She had a chronic flow of blood.
Instead of improving, she had grown worse.
Imagine twelve years of waking up to the same problem.
Twelve years of wondering whether tomorrow would finally be different.
Twelve years of spending money for another possibility.
Twelve years of your body becoming the thing around which your life must constantly reorganize itself.
And then Jesus came through town.
Maybe after years of having her condition define her, she wanted healing without another public explanation.
She reached through the bodies surrounding Christ and touched His garment.
Immediately, Mark says, the bleeding stopped.
A crowd can press against Jesus while one desperate person truly reaches for Him.
The thing she probably wished could remain anonymous.
And Jesus looked at this trembling woman and called her something beautiful.
The Greek of Mark 5:34 preserves His words:
Θυγάτηρ, ἡ πίστις σου σέσωκέν σε
Thygatēr, hē pistis sou sesōken se.
“Daughter, your faith has made you well.”

The verb σέσωκέν — sesōken comes from sōzō, a word whose semantic range includes saving, delivering, rescuing, and making well. In this context the woman's physical healing is unmistakably present; the language also carries the rich resonance of salvation and deliverance found elsewhere in the New Testament.
She approached Jesus carrying a condition involving blood.
She left hearing a word of relationship.
That is what Jesus does so beautifully.
He does not reduce people to the most uncomfortable chapter of their story.
Jesus knows the whole truth and still sees a human being standing before Him.
This does not mean Jesus minimizes sin.
The same Christ who receives sinners commands repentance.
Grace does not rename evil as good.
Grace tells the truth about evil and then announces that evil does not have to write the final sentence.
Some things we feel ashamed about are not sins at all.
They are simply parts of embodied human life.
Menstruation is not a moral failure.
Having a body is not sinful.
Sexual immorality is treated seriously throughout Scripture.
Jesus is not frightened by either category.
He knows how to remove false shame.
And He knows how to forgive real guilt.
Because if you call everything sin, you crush people beneath burdens God never gave them.
But if you call nothing sin, you leave guilty people without repentance—and therefore without understanding the wonder of forgiveness.
The Gospel does something infinitely better.
You may not need forgiveness for the thing someone taught you to be ashamed of.
And you may desperately need forgiveness for something you have been pretending isn't sin.
Jesus can meet you in both places.
That is why Christianity cannot afford to become a religion of polite pretending.
And ultimately a naked, bloodied Savior crucified publicly outside Jerusalem.
Scripture repeatedly walks straight into places respectable religion would rather cover with curtains.
Because redemption has nothing to redeem if everyone keeps pretending.
Maybe that is why some churches feel safe until somebody tells the truth.
“I am ashamed of what happened to me.”
“I am ashamed of what I did.”
“I don't know how to talk to my children about sex.”
“I have questions I was told Christians shouldn't ask.”
And suddenly the room gets quiet.
But that silence may be exactly where discipleship is needed most.
The church should be one of the safest places on earth to tell the truth—and one of the clearest places on earth to hear what God calls truth.
Because Jesus Christ did not come merely to make respectable people slightly more religious.
He came for people with histories.
People who have been sinned against.
People terrified that if the whole truth were known, love would disappear.
She told Him all the truth.
And after knowing the truth, He called her:
Maybe somebody needs to read that sentence twice.
The truth did not scare Jesus away.
Your truth will not surprise Him either.
The miscarriage you still cry about.
The memories that still make you feel dirty.
The questions you were too embarrassed to ask.
And where there is sin, His invitation is not to hide it but to repent.
Where there is woundedness, His invitation is not to manufacture guilt but to come into the light.
Where there is shame, His invitation is not endless self-punishment.
The cross already proves that Jesus is willing to enter the bloody reality of human brokenness.
Christian salvation does not happen because human beings cleaned themselves enough to approach God.
It happens because Christ came for sinners and gave Himself for them.
And grace is what rewrites it.
Maybe you have spent years thinking Christianity means becoming presentable enough that God will tolerate you.
The Gospel says something far more devastating to pride and far more healing to shame:
Repentance means we stop defending the darkness.
Faith means we stop trusting ourselves to rescue ourselves.
Grace means the Savior receives what we could never purchase.
Forgiveness means your worst sin does not possess greater saving power than Christ's cross.
Transformation means Jesus does not merely excuse you and abandon you unchanged.
He calls you out of darkness.
He teaches you to see your body not as a god to worship and not as garbage to despise, but as something belonging under the lordship of Christ.
So Christians should be able to talk about sex without becoming crude.
We should be able to talk about menstruation without making women ashamed.
We should be able to talk about semen without juvenile laughter.
We should be able to talk about childbirth without romanticizing every woman's experience.
We should be able to talk about sexual sin without pretending temptation itself makes someone beyond grace.
We should be able to confront pornography without treating addicts as subhuman.
We should be able to protect children without making their bodies mysterious sources of shame.
We should be able to tell abuse survivors clearly: what someone did to you is not the same thing as something you chose.
And we should be able to look sinners in the eyes and say:
Truth governed by holiness and saturated with grace.
And perhaps this is why this article needed to exist.
Because somewhere, someone is discovering for the first time that the Bible is far more honest about being human than the Christianity they encountered.
If that person is you, don't run from Scripture because someone mishandled it.
Learn the difference between ritual impurity and moral guilt.
Learn the difference between temptation and surrender.
Learn the difference between conviction and humiliation.
Learn the difference between biblical sexuality and cultural sexuality.
keep following the story until you reach Jesus.
Because every road worth following through Scripture ultimately forces us to confront Him.
And if this article exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to give strangers the details.
But you do not have to keep pretending either.
You may need these words again.
Scripture affirms the material support of Gospel ministry, while also teaching that Christian giving should come from the heart rather than coercion. Paul writes:
ἕκαστος καθὼς προῄρηται τῇ καρδίᾳ... μὴ... ἐξ ἀνάγκης
Each person should give as he has determined in his heart—not under compulsion (2 Corinthians 9:7).
If this ministry has fed you spiritually, consider helping us place the same truth in front of someone who has never seen it.
Because some ministry happens behind pulpits.
And sometimes it happens because one believer presses Share, and somewhere beyond their sight a wounded person finally encounters the Gospel at exactly the moment they were preparing to give up.
The Bible was never embarrassed by the reality of your body.
Jesus was never intimidated by the reality of your brokenness.
And the cross proves He was willing to bleed to redeem what sin had shattered.
So bring Him the whole truth.
Bring Him what you actually did.
Bring Him what was done to you.
Bring Him the version of the story you thought was too scandalous to say aloud.
Because the most unforgettable thing about the woman who told Jesus “all the truth” was not what she confessed about herself.
It was what Jesus called her afterward.
And maybe the chapter you have been most ashamed to let Jesus touch is the very chapter where you are about to discover how astonishing His grace really is.
Your scandal may explain yesterday—but in the hands of Jesus, it does not get to write your ending.
